originalGroup.material:
A word I knew on paper

Tuesday, 6 May

Our English club played a spelling game today. I had studied the word list carefully and recognised every word when I saw it. ____1____ Without the printed letters, I needed a moment to connect the sound with the word I knew.

On my first turn, I began spelling before the teacher had finished speaking. I had guessed the ending from the first sound. ____2____ The word she actually said was different from the one I expected.

I asked if I could hear it in a sentence. The extra context helped, and I tried again. This time I listened to the whole word before starting. ____3____ I still spoke slowly, but I reached the end without changing my answer halfway through.

After the game, my friend suggested practising from recordings as well as from a list. We took turns reading words while the other kept the paper hidden. ____4____ It was a useful way to prepare for what the game actually asked us to do.

A walk with one photograph

Saturday, 10 May

For our photography club, each member could submit only one picture from a walk by the river. I first thought the limit would make the task easy. ____1____ A bright boat, an old bridge and a reflection all seemed worth choosing.

I took several photographs but kept the camera down between them. Our teacher had asked us to watch the place as well as the screen. ____2____ Its movement changed the reflection I had been trying to capture.

My favourite first image had a clear bridge but also a stranger's face close to the camera. I checked the club's rules about using identifiable people in a public display and asked the teacher for guidance. ____3____ The bridge remained the subject without requiring that person's face in the picture.

Back in class, we compared what each single photograph left outside its frame. My chosen image did not show the boat or the whole riverbank. ____4____ The limit had made me think about selection, not just about collecting as many pictures as possible.

originalGroup.material:
Borrowing something with care

Borrowing an object begins with recognising that its owner may have plans you do not know about. Being friendly does not make another person's belongings automatically available. ____1____ A clear answer should come before you take the item away.

Ask about the arrangement

Give enough detail for the owner to decide. You might say, "____2____" The time and purpose make the request easier to answer than a vague promise to bring it back sometime.

Check the condition together

Notice any existing mark or loose part before use. ____3____ This protects both people from confusion about what changed while the item was away.

Keep the owner informed

If a problem occurs, explain it promptly rather than hoping it will disappear. ____4____ A person may be able to suggest what to do, and should not have to discover the problem only after the return.

____5____

Bring the object back at the agreed time and in the agreed way. Ask before leaving it somewhere different. A short confirmation that it has arrived safely completes the arrangement better than assuming the other person will eventually find it.

Joining an established group

Entering a group that already knows one another can feel awkward. Familiar jokes and routines may pass quickly, leaving a newcomer unsure how to take part. ____1____ You do not need to understand the group's whole history on the first afternoon.

Ask one useful question

A specific question can create an easier beginning than trying to impress everyone at once. You might say, "____2____" The answer gives you a practical place in the activity rather than only a place at the edge of the room.

Watch the ordinary routine

Notice how equipment is shared and how decisions are made. ____3____ An arrangement that looks obvious to a regular member may still need explaining to you.

Offer something manageable

Choose a contribution you can actually complete. ____4____ Taking on an enormous task to prove that you belong may create more uncertainty than a small reliable action.

____5____

One quiet meeting does not settle whether you fit the group. Return if the activity interests you, and notice whether questions and participation become easier. At the same time, take persistent unkindness or exclusion seriously rather than assuming that every difficulty is your own failure.
